opus-5.5.text:
I think success for us has a few layers, and they build on each other.

The first layer is the one people associate with us most: building mathematical superintelligence. That means a system that can reason about math at or beyond the level of the best humans, and, critically, can prove that its reasoning is correct. We care a lot about formal verification. When the system produces an answer, it should come with a proof checked by a machine, so you don't have to trust the model. You can trust the math. If we get there, that alone is a big deal for mathematics as a field. Problems that have been open for decades could become tractable, and mathematicians could work at a much higher level of abstraction.

But math was never the end goal by itself. The deeper reason we focus on it is that math underlies a huge amount of the world. Physics, engineering, computer science, software, chip design, cryptography: all of these depend on mathematical reasoning. So the second layer of success is when verified reasoning becomes something people use every day. Imagine software where the critical parts are proven correct, not just tested. Or engineering designs where you have guarantees instead of hoping you covered the edge cases. Today that kind of rigor is so expensive that only a few very high-stakes projects use it. If AI makes it cheap, it becomes the default.

The third layer is about trust in AI more broadly. As these systems get more capable, the question of whether we can believe their output gets more important. Hallucination isn't a cute quirk when the model is designing a bridge or writing flight-control code. I think verifiable reasoning is one of the cleanest answers to that problem. You don't argue with the model or rely on vibes. You check the proof.

So if I fast-forward ten years and see that mathematicians, scientists, and engineers routinely work with a system like ours, that it has helped solve problems people thought were out of reach, and that "is this verified?" has become a normal question to ask about AI output, I'd call that success. And honestly, if we helped accelerate science in a way that's measurable, where discoveries that would have taken a generation happen in a few years, that would be the thing I'm proudest of.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical superintelligence could make long-open problems tractable, but it does not identify solving all Millennium Prize problems as Harmonic’s ideal success.

fable-5.1.text:
Success for Harmonic, to me, is pretty simple to state and very hard to do: it's building a system that can do mathematics at the level of the best human mathematicians, and then going well beyond that. Not just solving competition problems, but generating genuinely new mathematics—new theorems, new proofs, new connections between fields that no human has seen before. And doing it in a way where every single step is formally verified, so you don't have to trust the model, you can check it.

The reason that matters, beyond mathematics itself, is that math is the foundation of basically all quantitative reasoning. If you can build a system that reasons reliably about math, you've built a system that can reason reliably, period. So the longer-term version of success is that the techniques we develop—verified reasoning, models that don't hallucinate because they're grounded in a formal system—end up in everything. In software, where you'd want provably correct code. In science, in engineering, in anything where being wrong is expensive.

If I had to pick a concrete milestone, it would be the day a working mathematician says, "I couldn't have proven this without Aristotle," and means it. Not as a tool that speeds up something they already knew how to do, but as a genuine collaborator that contributed an idea. When that becomes routine rather than remarkable, I'll feel like we've done what we set out to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a system that surpasses top human mathematicians and generates new mathematics, but it does not identify enabling mathematicians to solve all the Millennium Prize problems.

astra-6.text: For me, success would mean building a system that people can trust to reason through really hard problems—where it doesn’t just give you an answer that sounds plausible, but can show you why that answer is correct. And ultimately, I’d want that to help people discover things they couldn’t have discovered otherwise. If we can make that kind of reasoning broadly useful, that would be a meaningful success.

r001.rationale: The response describes trusted reasoning on hard problems and enabling new discoveries, but does not identify solving all the Millennium Prize problems as Harmonic’s ideal success.

sol-6.1.text: Success would be building AI that people can actually trust to reason correctly. Mathematics is a great starting point because you can check whether an answer is right—you can verify the proof. But the ambition goes beyond solving math problems. We want to help people tackle problems they couldn’t solve before, whether that’s a mathematician developing a new theory or an engineer designing something new. If we can make rigorous reasoning widely available and useful, that would be success.

r001.rationale: The response describes enabling people to tackle previously unsolved problems, including mathematical work, but does not identify solving all Millennium Prize problems as Harmonic’s ideal success.
